title: Unspoken Expectations are the Costliest Thing a Leader Never Says
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The author, opening with Neil Strauss's line that unspoken expectations are premeditated resentments, argues that leaders routinely judge people against standards they never stated. Drawing on Denise Rousseau's work on the psychological contract, the post explains that leaders and team members hold different assumptions, and that leaders overestimate how visible their intentions are. The result is predictable: team members violate expectations they never heard, and then feel treated unfairly, withdrawing discretionary effort. The usual advice to communicate more is called insufficient because communication is not the same as understanding. The proposed fix is narrower and more practical: clarify which decisions belong to the team member and which must follow set steps, since decision boundaries shape most other expectations.
points: Evaluating people against unstated expectations produces a justified sense of injustice, which turns into resentment and reduced effort.
Leaders systematically overrate how transparent and visible their standards are to others.
Telling leaders to set clear expectations is not enough because issuing communication does not guarantee understanding.
The practical lever is clarity about decision rights: what the team member decides versus what follows a scripted path.
The psychological contract can never be perfect, but clear decision boundaries shrink the room for resentment and build trust.
quotes: Leaders hold expectations for process and performance. When those expectations remain unstated but are still used to evaluate team members, the people being judged can feel a genuine sense of injustice.

Leaders often believe they are more transparent and explicit about their expectations than they objectively are. They also commonly overestimate how visible their intentions, priorities, and standards are to everyone else.

Team members, meanwhile, become resentful. They naturally view it as unfair to be evaluated against a set of expectations that were never communicated. That resentment, once it takes hold, shows up as a lack of discretionary effort and a general withdrawal from the leader.
The usual prescription for leaders is to communicate more and to “set clear expectations.” But that’s not as easy as it sounds, because communication and understanding are not the same thing.

The best leaders have learned that setting expectations isn’t about issuing instructions. It’s about drawing a clear line, early and often, between the decisions that belong to the team member and the ones that must follow a more scripted set of actions.

The psychological contract will never be perfect, because no leader can anticipate every assumption a team member carries into a role. But clarity about decision rights reduces the space for resentment to grow.
